sources.news_title: MAGA women are trapped in a paradox that leaves them 'doomed to fail'
sources.text:
GOP Rep. Lauren Boebert's failed reelection bid in the midterms capped off a "grim year for MAGA women," according to a new analysis from MS NOW, exposing how little they are getting from the paradox they are trapped in.
Writing for the outlet on Saturday morning, prolific commentator and journalist Amanda Marcotte broke down how Boebert attempted to sell herself as a "contradictory" vision of femininity to male conservatives.
"She titillated the right and annoyed the left with her over-the-top performance of a MAGA man’s contradictory fantasy of a woman who is both sexually liberated and a demure wife and mother," Marcotte explained. "Boebert was the forerunner to a type that has become ubiquitous in the Trump era: Republican women who gain fame and power by submitting to extreme beauty standards, while still insisting that they are good and pious ladies. Observers dubbed their combination of heavy makeup and rumored plastic surgery 'Mar-a-Lago face.'"
Marcotte argued further that Boebert's reelection loss to Democrat and retired Naval officer Eileen Laubacher in a supposedly safe red district showed why her particular "version of MAGA womanhood was always doomed to fail: The facade did not last long."
"It quickly became evident that hers was a turbulent marriage, and she ended it in 2023," she wrote. "Later that year, she was ejected from a showing of the musical 'Beetlejuice,' and camera footage showed her and her date apparently groping each other in front of other theatergoers. Facing a possible loss in her more swingy Colorado district, she relocated to a district nearby, winning a safe Republican seat in 2024. In the 2026 blue wave, though, even that wasn’t enough to save her seat."
She continued: "Boebert’s defeat capped off a year of such women being pushed out of power, either by voters or by male GOP leaders who needed handy scapegoats. Noem proclaimed the health of her 34-year marriage to Bryon Noem, until rumors of an affair with her aide Corey Lewandowski helped lead Trump to fire her. (Both Noem and Lewandowski denied having an affair.) Mace will be leaving Congress in January after a failed bid to be her state’s governor. Leavitt gave up her podium in August... Katie Zacharia lasted only a few days this year as White House press secretary, despite being showily Christian and sporting a standard Mar-a-Lago face."
Marcotte also suggested that, in trying to create a new paradigm for conservative women, people like Boebert instead "created an impossible and oppressive standard for" them, in which they are "expected to fulfill male fantasies without having even basic reproductive rights, much less freedom of their own."

sources.news_title: Lauren Boebert Loses Colorado House Seat to Democrat
sources.text:
Rep. Lauren Boebert is projected to lose her Colorado House seat to Democrat Eileen Laubacher, another Democratic flip that widens the party’s majority nearly two weeks after Election Day.
The Associated Press called Colorado’s 4th Congressional District for Laubacher on Friday afternoon after 99% of the ballots were counted, Fox News reported.
Laubacher held a slim 48.7% to 47.9% edge over Boebert. Libertarian candidate Douglas Mangeris took a little more than 3% of the vote and finished third.
The 39-year-old Republican was running for a fourth term. She served her first two terms in Colorado’s 3rd District before seeking a second term in the 4th.
The projection lands amid a broader Democratic surge that has already delivered the party a clear House majority.
Democrats now hold 256 House seats to Republicans’ 169. A majority requires 218.
That gap leaves the GOP well short of power in the next Congress. Several races nationwide remained uncalled nearly two weeks after Election Day.
Fox News described the Boebert result as part of a blue wave. Democrats flipped seats in Republican strongholds including Texas, Kansas, South Carolina, and Mississippi.
Colorado’s 4th became one more district to change hands under that pressure.
The final stretch was tight. With almost every ballot tallied, Laubacher’s lead stood at less than a percentage point.
Mangeris’s share exceeded the gap between the major-party candidates. In a race decided by tenths of a point, every ballot share mattered.
AP waited until 99% of the ballots were counted before making the call Friday afternoon. The delay fit a larger pattern of contests still unresolved long after voters cast their ballots.
Boebert built her reputation as a GOP firebrand during two terms in the 3rd District. She then moved to run in the 4th, seeking another term in a different Colorado seat.
The AP projection ends that bid. Laubacher, the Democratic challenger, is slated to take the seat once the result is finalized under state process.
Incoming House Minority Leader Rep. Jim Jordan, R-Ohio, has been discussing the GOP’s post-election posture, including priorities for the lame-duck session and Democratic lawfare threats, in appearances such as on “Hannity.”
With Republicans at 169 seats, the conference heads into the minority. The majority threshold of 218 is no longer in reach on the current tally.
The Boebert call came nearly two weeks after Election Day. Fox News noted that multiple races across the country still had not been decided at that point.
Late calls after heavy ballot processing leave voters waiting on final maps and committee power. In Colorado’s 4th, the AP decision followed the 99% threshold and the narrow percentage split among Laubacher, Boebert, and Mangeris.
Democrats’ 256-seat haul already exceeds the 218 needed to control the chamber. Flips in Texas, Kansas, South Carolina, and Mississippi added to the total alongside the Colorado projection.
Boebert’s projected defeat removes a high-profile conservative voice from the incoming House. The seat shifts to Laubacher on the AP call, tightening the arithmetic for Republicans still waiting on the remaining uncalled contests.
When competitive districts fall by less than a point and third-party shares exceed the margin, and when majorities are locked in while other races drag on for weeks, voters are entitled to fast counts, clear rules, and a House that reflects ballots without endless delay.

sources.text:
Lauren Boebert, a MAGA favorite, loses reelection bid in Colorado
|                            Getting your Trinity Audio player ready...                        | 
Rep. Lauren Boebert, a hard-line Republican, on Friday narrowly lost her bid for reelection in a conservative Colorado district, according to The Associated Press, an outcome that showed just how deeply Democrats had encroached into Republican territory this year.
Boebert, a fiery favorite of the MAGA movement, switched congressional districts a few years ago after her former district grew more competitive. But the change was not enough to keep her from being ousted by Eileen Laubacher, a Democrat.
Laubacher, a retired rear admiral in the Navy, was leading by more than 3,000 votes when The Associated Press called the race. Boebert said she called to congratulate Laubacher on Friday, four days after the Democrat declared victory, and hinted that she would not be retreating from the public eye.
“Public service was never meant to be a lifetime career, nor did I ever intend for it to be for myself,” Boebert said in a video posted on the social platform X. “Our founders expected representatives to serve and go back home.”
She added: “So I’m home, I am happy, I have peace, and this is not the last you’ll be hearing from me.”
Democrats flooded the airwaves in the district with more than $7 million worth of ads, outspending Republicans by more than 23 to 1, according to the media tracking firm AdImpact. Many of the ads fixed on Boebert’s polarizing nature and past scandals, with one calling her “uniquely unfit.” Another ad contrasted Laubacher’s profile as a Navy veteran and mother of five with headlines about Boebert.
“Lauren Boebert flips out over ‘Beetlejuice’ groping footage,’” the chyron read in one clip, referring to Boebert’s ejection from a Denver theater in 2023. Another showed Boebert cursing at the person filming.
“Like so many of us, Eileen is done with the extremists in both parties,” a narrator said in the ad, which was run by Laubacher’s campaign. “Maybe the best way to break through the noise is a little less talking and more listening.”
Democrats had viewed Boebert as vulnerable in the closing stretch of this year’s race, as her once-close alliance with Trump became a liability among voters who blamed his administration for high gas prices and other affordability concerns.
Boebert, first elected in 2020, broke with Trump at times during the past year, particularly over her calls to release files related to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. And she drew the president’s anger by campaigning for Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., who became a nuisance for Trump.
After the election, Boebert declined to blame Trump for Republicans’ blowout losses, though she said she was “very frustrated with the war.” She told reporters this week that the Trump administration should have gone further to deport immigrants who were in the United States illegally and that Republican lawmakers “could have done a lot more.”
Boebert said in the video posted on Friday that she went to Congress to “change how Washington works,” and that she felt she had achieved that goal.
“Those changes matter, and my hope is they will outlast any one member,” she said.
Laubacher ran on a centrist platform but hammered Boebert for her votes against resolutions directing Trump to end the war in Iran or seek congressional approval. She also made a promise to protect rural hospitals in the wake of Medicaid cuts.
Laubacher served in the National Security Council for two years during the Biden administration, and earlier in her career she worked as a Navy intelligence officer and served in the Navy Reserves. She was promoted to the rank of rear admiral in 2018.
“I don’t answer to a political party,” Laubacher said in a statement declaring victory Monday. “I answer to the people of the 4th District and I’ll work with anyone and everyone, including President Trump, Republicans, and Democrats to get things done for Colorado.”

Colorado’s Fourth Congressional District, long considered the state’s safest Republican seat, has flipped to the Democrats after a razor-thin result that took ten days to resolve.
DecisionDesk HQ called the race Friday afternoon for Democrat Eileen Laubacher, who finished with 48.79 percent of the vote to Republican incumbent Lauren Boebert’s 47.9 percent. Boebert lost by fewer than 3,000 votes. A Libertarian candidate drew more than 3 percent, a factor that may have cut into Boebert’s margin.
Laubacher, a retired Navy rear admiral and a former Republican, declared victory earlier in the week, before the official call, and has already been attending freshman orientation in Washington, D.C. This cycle’s loss ends her run in a district the GOP had counted on as its most secure in the state.

sources.news_title: Colorado 4th District Election: Eileen Laubacher Defeats Lauren Boebert in AP Call
sources.text:
The FINANCIAL — Democrat Eileen Laubacher has been declared the winner of the Colorado 4th District election, defeating Representative Lauren Boebert after days of ballot processing in a race that ended the three-term Republican’s tenure in the House but remains subject to Colorado’s formal canvass and certification process.
The Associated Press called the Nov. 3 contest for Laubacher on Friday. CBS News and Fox News also reported the call, while CNN and NBC News were among national outlets that reported the result after the regular ballot-counting deadlines had passed. The outcome gives Democrats a seat that Boebert had held since moving from Colorado’s 3rd District and winning the 4th District in 2024.
Colorado election pages continued to describe the figures as unofficial. The Douglas County election-results page, which posts districtwide totals for the contest, listed Laubacher with 186,244 votes, or 48.78%, and Boebert with 182,909, or 47.91%. Libertarian Douglas Mangeris had 12,618 votes, or 3.31%, among 381,771 votes counted.
Those figures placed Laubacher ahead by 3,335 votes, a margin of 0.87 percentage points. The contest was not called on election night because election offices were still processing eligible ballots, including cured ballots and ballots submitted by military and overseas voters. It remained unsettled in public reporting for more than a week after Election Day.
The media call and the election certificate are separate matters. The Colorado Clerks Association’s 2026 general-election calendar says counties must complete their canvasses and transmit their abstracts of votes to the secretary of state by Nov. 25. The secretary of state then compiles returns for statewide and congressional contests. Recounts that are required or requested are handled through the post-election timetable.
That sequence defined the latest development. Weld County Clerk and Recorder Carly Koppes told CBS Colorado that Friday was the last day for county clerks to count eligible ballots. CBS reported that the statewide result was not yet certified and that Colorado procedures still permit recount activity after the canvass.
Laubacher, a retired Navy rear admiral, will be the first Democrat to represent the district since 2008, according to Colorado Public Radio. The 4th District covers the Eastern Plains and portions of Front Range counties, including Douglas, Adams, Arapahoe, Larimer and Weld.
The race carried national weight because Boebert was among the best-known Republicans in the House. First elected in 2020 after defeating then-Representative Scott Tipton in a Republican primary, she built a national profile as an outspoken ally of President Donald Trump and as a member of the House Freedom Caucus.
Boebert represented the western-slope 3rd District for two terms. After a close 2022 re-election there, she announced in late 2023 that she would run in the 4th District, a more Republican-leaning seat that became open after Representative Ken Buck resigned. She won the district in 2024 with 53.6% of the vote, CBS Colorado reported.
The 4th District had been regarded as one of Colorado’s strongest Republican House seats. When its boundaries were drawn after the 2020 census, Republicans had an average advantage of about 25 percentage points, Colorado Public Radio reported. The Associated Press reported that Republicans carried the district by more than 18 percentage points in 2024.
Laubacher’s win changes that recent record. Douglas County, the district’s largest population center, posted a local result that gave Laubacher 53.87% to Boebert’s 43.08%. Boebert won a number of less-populous rural counties, but the reported districtwide tally left Laubacher ahead.
Colorado’s process separates the election officials’ work from the calls made by news organizations. Clerks publish unofficial totals while they finish ballot review, reconcile the number of ballots cast and conduct audits. The Associated Press and television networks make race calls when their assessments find that outstanding ballots are not sufficient to change the leader. Neither a call nor a concession replaces the statutory canvass.
The schedule gives voters time to correct certain ballot problems. The clerks’ association said voters with qualifying signature or identification issues had through Nov. 12 to cure ballots. Counties then review provisional ballots, complete auditing and prepare the abstract of votes that will be sent to the secretary of state. Those procedures are routine steps in a Colorado election and remain under way after a projected result is announced.
Colorado also conducts risk-limiting audits. Boulder County’s election office described the process as a comparison of a sample of paper ballots with the digital tally, designed to test whether the reported outcome reflects the votes cast. Boulder County is outside the 4th District, but its description reflects the statewide audit framework used in the post-election period.
Laubacher had already joined other incoming House members in Washington for orientation earlier in the week. Colorado Public Radio reported that she described her campaign as a commitment to representation rooted in the district and its daily concerns. Her victory puts a former senior Navy officer into a district that had not sent a Democrat to Congress for nearly two decades.
Boebert acknowledged the outcome after the AP call. In a video posted Friday, she said she had called Laubacher to congratulate her, according to the Associated Press. At the Capitol this week, as Republican losses accumulated nationally, Boebert said, “We collectively failed,” and said voters had made a judgment about the party’s governing record.
The results also affect the incoming House. Fox News reported that Democrats will hold 256 seats to Republicans’ 169 as races now called are reflected, above the 218 seats needed for a majority. The network said several races elsewhere in the country still had not been called Friday.
For Boebert, the result closes a congressional career that began with an upset primary victory in 2020 and continued through two districts, three general-election victories and a national political profile that often made her a focus of party debates. Her move to the 4th District was meant to place her in a more favorable electoral environment; Friday’s call showed that the district’s recent voting pattern did not hold in this contest.
For Laubacher, the next stage is administrative rather than electoral. County canvass boards will review records and certify the abstracts they submit. The secretary of state will then compile the returns and issue the state’s certified outcome for the congressional race. The final certified vote totals may differ from the unofficial figures currently displayed, though the AP call was based on Laubacher’s sustained lead after the final regular counting deadlines.
The distinction remains important. Colorado election officials have not yet issued the final certificate for the 4th District. But by Friday evening, the political result was clear: Laubacher had more votes in the reported districtwide count, the AP and major television news organizations had called the race, and Boebert had publicly congratulated the Democrat who is expected to replace her in January if the state’s certification confirms the result.

MAGA firebrand Lauren Boebert has been forced out of Congress after losing her re-election bid to Democrat Eileen Laubacher in a closely fought race overshadowed by years of controversy.
The Associated Press called the contest more than a week after the midterm elections, as a nationwide “bluenami” delivered major gains for Democrats.
With 99 percent of the vote counted, Boebert was trailing Laubacher by just over 3,000 ballots. Laubacher secured 49.8 percent, compared with Boebert’s 47.9 percent.

It also makes clear that the later canvass and recount calendar is separate from the deadline for completing the count itself. Interested parties may request a recount beginning November 13, but the state does not finish its formal canvass until later in the month.
In other words, Friday was the point at which the remaining cure, military and overseas ballot deadlines had run their course and counties had to report the completed tabulation that election desks needed for a final projection.
That final influx was not enough to erase Laubacher’s lead.
Colorado Public Radio reported earlier in the week that Laubacher was already ahead by more than 3,000 votes, a margin outside the range that would trigger an automatic recount under Colorado law.
Both women had traveled to Washington while the result remained unresolved. Laubacher attended orientation for incoming House members, while Boebert continued participating in congressional business and waited for the count.
CPR also noted that Laubacher considered herself the winner before the AP made its call, while Boebert maintained that the outstanding ballot process needed to finish. That gap between political reality and a definitive election call explains why the race remained in limbo for days after other networks projected the outcome.
A Colorado outlet posted the updated Friday margin as the race was called:
AP CALLS CD-4: Eileen Laubacher defeats Rep. Lauren Boebert, 187,518 to 184,066, a margin of 3,452 votes.
— Rocky Mountain Voice (@TheRMVoice) November 13, 2026
The scale of the upset is difficult to overstate.
Boebert won this district in 2024 by more than 50,000 votes. President Trump carried it by more than 18 percentage points that same year.
This was not a suburban swing seat that Republicans expected to lose. It was the most Republican-friendly congressional district in Colorado.
But the money and the movement in Douglas County told a different story.
Axios Douglas County reported that Laubacher outraised Boebert by more than 10-to-1 through June and built an advantage of roughly 22,000 votes in Douglas County.
The outlet noted that Republicans had carried that county by nearly 26,500 votes just four years earlier.
Axios described the result as a stunning upset in a longtime Republican stronghold. Laubacher’s advantage in the populous Denver suburbs overwhelmed Boebert’s support across the Eastern Plains and transformed a district that had barely drawn national attention at the start of the cycle.
The fundraising gap helped make that possible. Laubacher entered the final stretch with the resources to define the race, while Boebert found herself defending terrain that Republicans had treated as safely red.
That swing helped produce the district’s first Democratic member of Congress in 18 years.
Laubacher, a retired Navy rear admiral and first-time candidate, will replace a congresswoman who became a national figure almost immediately after entering the House in 2021.
Boebert built her reputation as a relentless defender of the Second Amendment, a fierce critic of the Biden administration and one of President Trump’s most visible allies on Capitol Hill.
Trisha Calvarese, the Democrat Boebert defeated in 2024, congratulated Laubacher while also crediting Boebert for signing the petition that forced a House vote on releasing the Epstein files:
Congratulations to Eileen Laubacher and her team. Respect to Rep. Lauren Boebert for signing the Epstein discharge petition.
— Trisha Calvarese (@trisha4colorado) November 13, 2026
She also survived one of the closest House races in America in 2022, defeating Democrat Adam Frisch by only 546 votes in her former district.
Two years later, the district switch gave her a double-digit victory and appeared to reset her political future.
Now that future is uncertain.
Fox reported that Democrats hold 256 House seats to the Republicans’ 169, with several races still unresolved. A party needs 218 seats for control.
Boebert’s loss is therefore bigger than one personality or one district.
It is another piece of a brutal midterm map for the GOP, and it raises hard questions about how a Republican incumbent lost a district President Trump had carried so comfortably only two years earlier.
The earlier calls were projections.
Friday’s AP call is the update that closes the race: Eileen Laubacher is projected to win, Lauren Boebert is projected to lose, and Colorado’s 4th Congressional District is flipping from Republican to Democrat.
This is a Guest Post from our friends over at WLTReport. View the original article here.

Lauren Boebert, once a MAGA star, loses her Colorado seat
- Published
Lauren Boebert, the Republican representative from Colorado who rose to national fame as one of Donald Trump's biggest cheerleaders, has lost her seat in Congress.
The race was too close to call on election night last week, but after every vote was counted the Democrat Eileen Laubacher has been declared the winner by the AP news agency.
It means Boebert, who was one of the most vocal conservatives in the House of Representatives, will not serve a fourth term.
The 39-year-old was one of the faces of Trump's "Make America Great Again" - or MAGA - movement, when she burst on to the Colorado political scene at the end of 2019.
Like the president, she was not a career politician. Boebert first made headlines when she encouraged staff at her restaurant Shooters, located in a small Colorado town named Rifle, to openly carry firearms.
Her rallies focused on gun rights and fighting - fighting Democrats, fighting the establishment, fighting illegal immigration or fighting anyone or anything that could be deemed "woke".
"Speaking after Lauren Boebert was like the band that played after the Beatles - no-one remembered them," said Republican state representative Matt Soper, now Colorado's most senior Republican legislator.
He first met Boebert and her then-husband, Jayson, when she was gathering signatures for a state-voting initiative.
She arrived in jeans with a Glock on her hip, her husband "looking like a classic oilman" in blue jeans, boots, cowboy hat and belt buckle, Soper told the BBC.
It played well with her Western Colorado constituency - a mix of ranches, farms and tough terrain with a smattering of ski towns - which Trump won with 53% of the vote in 2016.
Those same voters embraced Boebert in the lead-up to the 2020 election, helping her unseat the five-term Republican incumbent in the party's primary.
Boebert earned her high school equivalency diploma right before that victory, then won the seat in November, just before her 34th birthday.
It was the start of a political career Soper did not anticipate after that first meeting with her and her spouse.
"If I had been told, you know, they're going to make not just national headlines, but international headlines, for years, and Lauren will be a member of Congress for six years, I mean, I would have put no money on that bet," he said.
Once in Congress, Boebert garnered constant airtime with her aggressive pro-Trump rhetoric. Along with fellow political provocateurs like Marjorie Taylor Greene, she established herself as one of the most outspoken MAGA cheerleaders.
Perhaps most notably, she joined Greene in heckling President Joe Biden during his 2022 State of the Union address.
But that knack for the limelight began to work against Boebert at home.
"I think, as that national profile grew, it made it much harder for her to be able to maintain that small-town fighter narrative that she had relied on," Justin Gollob, a political science professor at Colorado Mesa University, told the BBC.
Waning enthusiasm for Boebert became glaringly apparent in 2022, when a Democrat from Aspen challenged her for her seat and nearly won. Boebert eked out a victory by just 546 votes.
Colorado voters had initially liked Boebert's "straight talk and her direct, down-the-barrel approach" as well as her conservative Christian views, said Rich Wyatt, a county Republican chairman in Colorado and former reality star who served time in prison for tax fraud.
But that narrative became harder for her to maintain as the congresswomen was beset by controversies that were personal, not political.
She filed for divorce from her husband and, five months later, footage of Boebert and a man being kicked out of a Denver performance of the musical Beetlejuice went viral.
Staff accused the politician of vaping, taking pictures and "causing a disturbance".
Footage released by the theatre showed Boebert, in a gold cocktail dress, arguing with staff before twirling and dancing with her date upon ejection.
An incident report claimed she had told staff "do you know who I am?" and "I will be contacting the mayor," the Denver Post reported.
That December - facing another matchup with Adam Frisch, the former Aspen Democratic councilman who nearly unseated her - Boebert announced she would be switching districts altogether. She moved across the state to Colorado's easternmost constituency, which voted reliably Republican.
With Trump's endorsement, Boebert won the seat in 2024.
But she turned on the president during his second term in office, when she became one of four House Republicans pushing for the full release of the Epstein files.
Suddenly, her biggest champion was no longer in her corner.
The next month, Trump vetoed a water bill Boebert had sponsored. As she sought re-election this year, he took aim at her on social media.
The president invited candidates to run against her in the primary (though the deadline had already passed) and called his former cheerleader "dumb" and "weak-minded".
Trump eventually endorsed Boebert for the race, but Democrats had found a strong moderate candidate to take her on - Navy veteran Eileen Laubacher, who retired in 2024 as a two-star rear admiral.
Like several other Democrats who have emerged victorious after the 2026 midterms, Laubacher's win is as much about her qualities as a candidate - she was a former Republican with strong appeal to middle-ground voters - as it was a rebuke of Boebert's time in office.
Peggy Lozen, a constituent who voted for Trump in 2016 but not after that, was thrilled to see Boebert go. She had been turned off by the representative since her State of the Union stunt in 2022.
"I was sick over that," the 72-year-old told BBC. "I was raised in an era where you respect everyone, regardless of their opinion, and especially the president of the United States."
The mother of a veteran, she voted for the rear admiral and displayed a sign of support in her yard.
"You can't even compare the two," she said of Laubacher and Boebert.
While it remains to be seen what Boebert does next, there is a consensus among both politicians and the public that she is unlikely to vanish altogether.
"I'll leave you with this," Wyatt said: "You haven't seen the end of Lauren Boebert."

Democrat Eileen Laubacher topples Lauren Boebert in Colorado’s 4th CD
Democrat Eileen Laubacher has defeated Republican U.S. Rep. Lauren Boebert in Colorado’s 4th Congressional District, delivering a major upset in the state’s safest GOP seat and leaving just one Republican in the state’s 10-member federal delegation.
The Associated Press called the race just before 1 p.m. Friday, after county election officials posted final, unofficial vote totals 10 days after polls closed. With an estimated 99% of the vote tallied, Laubacher held a 3,525-vote lead over Boebert out of just under 385,000 votes counted, for a margin of 0.91%.
Recommended Stories
Laubacher claimed victory Monday after CNN projected she would win, but Boebert insisted it was too early to declare the race finished while thousands of ballots remained outstanding.
“I’m honored by the trust the people of Colorado’s 4th District have placed in me,” Laubacher said in a statement. “This campaign was never about party labels. It was about putting people first.”
“This victory is historic. But making history means nothing if we don’t make a difference,” Laubacher continued. “My focus is simple: lower costs, protect healthcare, strengthen rural communities, take on corruption in both parties, and hold Washington accountable.”
Laubacher attended orientation activities for new House members this week in Washington, where she was reportedly greeted with sustained applause from fellow Democrats for ousting the incumbent in one of the reddest districts to flip in this year’s midterms. Two years ago, President Donald Trump carried its electorate by an 18-point margin.
Boebert said Monday in an online video that her opponent and others had wanted to “prematurely declare victory” before the deadline to finish counting.
“Declaring victory now is like icing a cake before it comes out of the oven,” she said, adding that she was grateful to the voters and her campaign team.
“Regardless of the final outcome, we will move forward to future victories together,” she said. “We’ll make sure that every eligible vote is counted and every single voice is heard before we take any next steps.”
In a fundraising email sent to her supporters the same day, Boebert said: “Our legal team expects a recount will happen one way or another, and we’re preparing for it NOW.”
Laubacher’s lead is too wide to trigger an automatic recount under state law, which requires that the difference between the top two candidates be 0.5% or less of the highest vote-getter’s total. That means the difference would have to be under 1,000 votes — less than one-third of Laubacher’s winning margin.
Either candidate or a political organization can request a recount no matter the margin, but they’ll have to pay for it. Boebert told reporters in Washington earlier in the week that she didn’t expect to pay for one.
Before the race was called, Boebert also said that if she lost, she didn’t plan to seek a rematch.
On Friday, Laubacher had secured 48.8% of the vote, ahead of Boebert at 47.89%. Libertarian Douglas Mangeris trailed with 3.31%.
County clerks had until just before midnight Thursday night to receive cured and military and overseas ballots. Election officials also withheld an unspecified number of ballots to include in the final count to preserve ballot anonymity — so voters’ choices wouldn’t be apparent in counties where only a handful of late-arriving ballots would be added to the totals.
A lawyer for Boebert’s campaign, former Republican Secretary of State Scott Gessler, called it “irresponsible” to declare a winner days before all the ballots had been counted.
“Every vote should be counted, and every vote should matter,” Gessler said in a statement Boebert’s campaign released.
Laubacher led Boebert since election night, but her margin narrowed in the days since, while county election officials continued to update the results. After closing to a roughly 3,000-vote advantage late last week, however, Laubacher maintained and even grew her margin as returns trickled in.
After several days with only a couple hundred votes added to the totals, clerks posted the remaining vote totals on Friday, including “cured” and overseas ballots that had to be received by 11:59 p.m. Thursday night. Voters can “cure” ballots by fixing signature or other discrepancies, while military and overseas ballots must be postmarked by 7 p.m. Nov. 3 in order to be counted.
Boebert’s loss means Colorado will be sending seven Democrats and just one Republican to the U.S. House of Representatives next year, following a massive blue wave in this year’s midterm elections that swept Republicans from office across the country and saw Democrats win control of both chambers of Congress.
In Colorado, Democrats unseated three incumbent Republican House members. In addition to Boebert, U.S. Rep, Gabe Evans fell to Manny Rutinel by nearly 15 points in the 8th Congressional District, and Jessica Killin defeated U.S. Rep. Jeff Crank by an almost 5-point margin in the 5th Congressional District, which has never before elected a Democrat.
The lone Republican left standing in this year’s Colorado midterms is U.S. Rep. Jeff Hurd, who fended off a challenge from Democrat Dwayne Romero by nearly 2 points in the 3rd Congressional District.
When lawmakers are sworn in at the beginning of next year, Democrats stand to hold the largest majority in the state’s congressional delegation since 1940, when Democrats held all four of Colorado’s House seats and both Senate seats.
Both of the state’s U.S. senators are Democrats — Michael Bennet, who is serving his third full term, and John Hickenlooper, who was elected to a second term by a wide margin on Nov. 3.
Laubacher’s win ends the congressional tenure of the state’s senior and most prominent Republican, marked by Boebert’s unconventional approach and high-profile clashes with Democrats and members of her own party, including Trump.
The 58-year-old Laubacher, a first-time candidate, is a retired U.S. Navy rear admiral and former National Security Council official. She said she ran to bring more mature representation to the district, including finding common ground on affordability, healthcare and housing.
Laubacher moved into the district last summer from the nearby Ken Caryl neighborhood, where she and her husband raised their family, and now lives in Highlands Ranch.
Boebert, 39, burst onto the political scene in late 2019 when she confronted then-presidential candidate Beto O’Rourke over the Texas Democrat’s proposal to confiscate firearms.
“Hell no, you won’t take away our guns!” Boebert told O’Rourke at a campaign stop in Aurora, garnering national headlines.
A few months later, Boebert launched a primary challenge against five-term U.S. Rep. Scott Tipton. The owner of Shooters Grill, a gun-themed restaurant in Rifle, Boebert vowed to take a more aggressive stance against “all the left-wing lunatics” than the more moderate incumbent had.
Boebert surprised Tipton in the 2020 primary, becoming the first Colorado candidate to unseat an incumbent House member in a primary in 48 years. She went on to win election to the House with Trump’s endorsement.
Two years later, Boebert came within 546 votes of losing the seat to Democrat Adam Frisch.
Nearly a year before the 2024 election — with Frisch seeking a rematch while posting record fundraising hauls and Boebert’s own internal polls showing she was vulnerable — Boebert moved across the state to run for another term in the more solidly Republican 4th Congressional District after the seat’s GOP incumbent announced he wouldn’t seek another term.
Boebert’s move in late 2023 came on the heels of a major controversy that engulfed the Republican after she and a male companion were ejected from a Denver performance of the musical “Beetlejuice” for inappropriate behavior.
She survived a crowded primary in the new district and beat Democratic nominee Trisha Calvarese by an 11-point margin. Her campaigns have focused on supporting Trump, border security, boosting fossil fuel production and reducing government spending and federal regulation.
Anchored by Douglas County, the 4th CD covers all or parts of 21 counties, including Colorado’s Eastern Plains and the Loveland area. The Republicans who held the seat before Boebert routinely won with margins topping 20 percentage points.
According to vote totals posted by the Colorado Secretary of State’s Office, Laubacher carried the district’s more densely populated portions in Douglas, Larimer and Arapahoe counties, while Boebert led in the district’s smaller, rural counties.
The 4th CD’s voters have elected a Democrat only once in the modern era, in 2008, when the district included nearly all of Larimer and Weld counties, and extended into Fort Collins and Greeley, making it more competitive than it’s been since subsequent rounds of redistricting.
In the week before the election, national forecasters moved the district into the “leans Republican” category — one step away from a “toss-up” — suggesting the race was more up for grabs than the district’s makeup and electoral history implied.
Hours before Laubacher claimed victory, Attorney General Phil Weiser, Colorado’s Democratic governor-elect, applauded a CNN story projecting that Boebert had lost her bid for reelection.
“This is what democracy looks like!” Weiser said on X, adding that Laubacher “is the real deal, worked hard to earn the trust of the people of the 4th Congressional District, and will be an outstanding member of Congress.”

sources.news_title: Lauren Boebert loses her 4th Congressional District seat to Democratic challenger Eileen Laubacher
sources.text:
HIGHLANDS RANCH — U.S. Rep. Lauren Boebert has lost her reelection bid in the Colorado congressional district most favorable to Republicans, becoming one of the highest-profile victims of an election that upended the GOP across the country.
The lighting rod Republican congresswoman, who served in Congress for six years through personal and political missteps that made for embarrassing headlines, was ousted by Eileen Laubacher, a moderate Democrat who was previously a Republican.
The race, separated by fewer than 4,000 votes, was called by The Associated Press at 12:53 p.m. on Friday, 10 days after the election, when Laubacher, a retired Navy rear admiral, had 48.8% and Boebert had 47.9% of the votes tallied. Douglas Mangeris of the Libertarian Party was in third place with 3.3%.
Laubacher’s victory marks only the second time since 1973 that a Democrat has won in Colorado’s 4th Congressional District, which spans the Eastern Plains into Douglas County and Loveland. With her win, just one Republican in the state’s congressional delegation — Rep. Jeff Hurd of Grand Junction — survived the blue wave, as Democrats flipped three other seats.
Just two years ago, Boebert, who had on-again-off-again political favor with President Donald Trump, beat her Democratic opponent in the 4th District by more than 11 percentage points.
The race dragged on for over a week as Boebert’s campaign waited for the last remaining votes to be counted, including military and overseas ballots and ballots with signature problems or other discrepancies that voters are able to fix after the election.
Laubacher claimed victory Monday after CNN projected she would win the race.
“This victory is historic,” she said in a news release. “But making history means nothing if we don’t make a difference. My focus is simple: lower costs, protect healthcare, strengthen rural communities, take on corruption in both parties, and hold Washington accountable.”
Laubacher, 58, of Highlands Ranch, said she was drawn to run for office because she was fed up with the extremes in both parties. She served in the U.S. Navy for 34 years, including a deployment to Afghanistan and working as an intelligence officer and as a member of the National Security Council. She worked on South Asia policy under President Joe Biden, and retired in 2024 as a rear admiral.
Laubacher, who was running for office for the first time and pitched herself as a drama-free alternative, far out-raised the incumbent congresswoman — $13.7 million through mid-October compared with Boebert’s $1.2 million.
On election night, Laubacher spoke to cheering supporters on a chilly rooftop patio of a Highlands Ranch pub, sounding hopeful.
“Integrity matters. Character matters. Truth matters, and public service should always be about what you can do for other people, not for what you do for yourself,” Laubacher said just after midnight on Nov. 4. “Those things were worth fighting for when we started.”
Boebert was first elected to represent the 4th District in 2024, after moving to Windsor. Before that, she represented the 3rd Congressional District in western Colorado for two terms.
Private polling obtained by The Sun showed Boebert, 39, was in for a tight race but that the 4th District, once considered solidly Republican, still favored the GOP.
However, continued personal issues for the congresswoman made for difficult headlines leading up to Election Day, including appearing in court to ask for leniency for her son, who faced charges of child abuse and sexual exploitation.
Earlier this year, Trump castigated Boebert for splitting with him on the release of files related to Jeffrey Epstien, the disgraced financier accused of sex crimes. Trump called Boebert “dumb” and “weak-minded” because she campaigned for U.S. Rep. Thomas Massie, a Kentucky Republican and a Trump critic.
But four days before the election — in the clearest sign the congresswoman was in trouble — he endorsed Boebert, calling her a “MAGA Warrior” in a social media post.
Two years ago, Boebert was reelected by 11.6 percentage points in the 4th District with 53% of the vote, even after enduring public mockery for being escorted out of a 2023 performance of the musical “Beetlejuice,” where she and a date were accused of taking photographs, groping each other and vaping in the theater.
About two months after the theater incident, she announced she was moving to the 4th District from the 3rd District, where she had won reelection in 2022 by just 546 votes.
Boebert’s near-loss in 2022 was attributed to her blunders in Congress. She and her team feared the “Beetlejuice” incident would make running again in the 3rd District an impossibility, looking to the 4th District — and its more conservative electorate — as a political safety net.
But while the “Beetlejuice” drama didn’t pose much of a problem for Boebert in 2024, it was resurfaced this fall in attack ads from a Democratic super PAC that invested $1.5 million in its effort to oust Boebert from Congress.
Boebert didn’t get much super PAC help in her reelection bid. A group tied to the House Freedom Caucus, of which Boebert is a member, spent about $450,000 on the race on the congresswoman’s behalf.
On election night, Boebert encouraged supporters to have fun as they waited for more results to come in at a large sports bar in Windsor. As a country band played, she danced in front of the stage and posed for photos with people while also keeping a close eye on results, periodically checking a tablet computer at her table.
She told her supporters that God would remain in charge no matter who won and told the Exodus story about God splitting the Red Sea for the Israelites fleeing Egypt.
“Tonight I’m telling you no matter what happens in our country and in our state, you have the authority given unto you to go forward. You can split that Red Sea and walk through on dry land because God is still the way maker and we are his people when we are called to greatness,” she said.
In Highlands Ranch, Laubacher supporters gathered on election night at a pub in the town center, eating burgers and fries and watching election returns on multiple televisions.
Democrats in Douglas County cheered as races across the state and country were called for Democrats, and the crowd hung on until midnight in the hopes that another round of election returns would be enough to call the race in Laubacher’s favor.
Krischele Gill, a stay-at-home mother who knocked on more than 1,200 doors for Laubacher and stayed at the party late into the night, said she was impressed by Laubacher’s integrity, and the fact that she spent more time listening to people than talking about herself.
“People are tired of the chaos that Boebert brings to the district and to Congress in general,” she said. “They see Eileen as the adult in the room. She is willing to step up and hold people accountable.”
In a fiery debate during the campaign, Laubacher criticized Boebert for voting against four bills that support veterans, including the PACT Act to expand healthcare in the Department of Veterans Affairs, and for voting for the war in Iran.
Boebert, meanwhile, accused Laubacher of being involved in the Hunter Biden laptop controversy, alleging she was part of a cover-up related to the emails found on the laptop of Biden’s son. Laubacher said she was not involved with the laptop investigation.
The candidates have starkly different views on immigration. Laubacher said there “should be a way for hardworking people who are paying taxes, such as those who have applied for asylum and those who previously had protected status, to try to become permanent residents.” Boebert said the Trump administration’s immigration policies are making the country safer and that, “If you’re in our country illegally, then you have to leave.”
Regarding Medicaid work requirements, Laubacher said she generally supports the requirements but that the law’s paperwork demands are excessive and that people are losing healthcare coverage because of the paperwork. Boebert said work requirements should have been enacted a long time ago because “we do not need able-bodied adults sitting at home receiving benefits that should be going to our more vulnerable populations.”
In an interview with 9News after Election Day, with her reelection in doubt, Boebert said she wasn’t surprised by the result. She said the war in Iran was in large part to blame.
“We absolutely made promises as a party that have not been upheld,” she said. “I have done everything that I can to uphold the promises that I make to my voters. I have complete peace about the job that I have done. I believe that me and my team did all that we could.”
Boebert vowed to continue in public service if she didn’t get reelected to Congress.
“I’m still a Coloradan, I’m still an American,” she told 9News. “We’re going to still keep fighting for this state.”
Colorado Sun staff writer Jesse Paul contributed to this report.

Rep. Lauren Boebert loses to Democrat Eileen Laubacher in Colorado's 4th Congressional District
Published in Political News
DENVER — Democrat Eileen Laubacher unseated U.S. Rep. Lauren Boebert in Colorado’s 4th Congressional District as final vote-counting ended Friday, 10 days after the polls closed.
The Associated Press called the race for Laubacher, a retired Naval rear admiral, at 12:53 p.m. in Colorado’s most right-leaning district. The vote showed Laubacher with 48.8% of the vote to Boebert’s 47.9%.
Laubacher had declared victory Monday in the tight race against Boebert, the conservative firebrand whose political fortunes were among those upended by the overwhelming blue wave that propelled Democrats to House and Senate majorities last week.
“It’s up to me to now deliver for people and make the changes that are going to improve their lives,” Laubacher said in an interview with The Denver Post on Monday.
Boebert did not concede then, though, and shared a video on social media in which she stressed that there were still ballots, including from overseas and the military, that needed to be counted or “cured” of signature discrepancies by Friday’s deadline.
“We’ll make sure every eligible vote is counted and that every single voice is heard before we take any next steps,” Boebert said Monday.
Scott Gessler, an attorney for Boebert’s campaign, said in a statement last week that her campaign staff was “fighting for every vote.” He said, without citing specifics, that the campaign was “investigating some very unusual voting patterns and expect this election to head to a recount, one way or another.”
Boebert, in her video to supporters, did not raise any claims of voting irregularities.
Laubacher is a former Republican who only recently became a Democrat. She moved to Highlands Ranch with her husband two years ago and describes herself as politically moderate. “I’ve never been a straight-party ticket voter — I’ve never felt either party matched me perfectly,” she said Monday.
Boebert moved to Windsor in the 4th Congressional District two years ago after nearly losing the seat she had held for two terms in the 3rd Congressional District on the Western Slope.
In her current race, results show Laubacher carried the more urban — and more populated — corners of the 4th District, including Douglas, Larimer and Arapahoe counties, while Boebert led in most rural counties, including Weld.
Laubacher’s victory leaves Democrats with a 7-1 majority among Colorado’s House seats, as last week’s election also saw Manny Rutinel unseat Rep. Gabe Evans and Jessica Killin defeat Rep. Jeff Crank.
Rep. Jeff Hurd was the only incumbent Colorado Republican in Congress to be reelected.

Lauren Boebert says losing her election could be “almost liberating,” even as she is not ready to concede her race. Speaking to TMZ on Capitol Hill, she joked about colleagues who won their races, saying she wants to “offer condolences” to some of them.
The comments came as Democrat Eileen Laubacher declared victory on Monday in Colorado’s 4th Congressional District. As reported by The Denver Post, Laubacher, a retired Navy rear admiral, holds a 48.8% to 47.9% lead, a margin just under 1 percentage point that is not close enough to trigger an automatic recount.
More than 98% of votes in the district have been counted, with a small number of ballots remaining, including military and overseas votes. CNN has projected Laubacher as the winner, though the Associated Press had not called the race as of Monday evening, The Colorado Sun reported.
Boebert isn’t giving up on the remaining ballots just yet
Boebert insists “the fat lady ain’t sung yet,” pointing to thousands of ballots still being counted. She said that if those ballots change the outcome, then so be it, and if they do not, she will accept the results.
In a video on social media, Boebert said “CNN and the Democrats” had called the race prematurely, noting that votes are still left to be counted or “cured” of signature discrepancies. She compared declaring victory now to “icing a cake before it comes out of the oven.”
Boebert also said, “We’ll make sure every eligible vote is counted and that every single voice is heard before we take any next steps.” She did not repeat vague claims of possible voting irregularities that a campaign attorney had made last week.
Laubacher was in Washington, D.C., on Monday for new member orientation while the remaining votes were still being counted. Adam Frisch, another Democratic opponent of Boebert’s, did the same in 2022 while more than 1,000 votes behind her, and he ultimately lost that election.

Laubacher is a former Republican who only recently became a Democrat, and she moved to Highlands Ranch with her husband two years ago. She told a local publication in October that she is “a very moderate person” and has “never been a straight-party ticket voter.” She said she would work with anyone to pass “meaningful legislation,” such as rolling back President Donald Trump’s tariffs, ending the war in Iran, and “cracking down on corruption.”
The 4th District is the most Republican-leaning of Colorado’s eight congressional districts, and voters there have put a Democrat in the seat only once in the last 53 years. The race comes amid what many are calling a “blue wave” that hit President Trump’s coalition last week.
Boebert moved to Windsor in the 4th District two years ago after nearly losing her seat in the Western Slope’s 3rd Congressional District. She came to prominence in 2019 as the owner of the now-defunct Shooters Grill in Rifle, where staff carried guns, and went on to beat longtime Republican incumbent Scott Tipton in the GOP primary.
In September 2023, she was removed from a performance of “Beetlejuice” at Denver’s Buell Theatre after patrons complained about her vaping and filming the show. She apologized, but her standing with 3rd District constituents had fallen far enough that she chose to move to the more conservative 4th District.
During her time in Congress, Boebert helped shepherd a bipartisan endangered fish recovery reauthorization into law, and then-President Joe Biden signed her CONVEY Act. After Trump returned to the White House in January 2025, she was a reliable ally, though she pushed to have the Epstein files released, something the president initially resisted.

Trump posted on Truth Social in May urging people to run against Boebert, calling her “weak-minded” and a “carpetbagger,” but he endorsed her three days before the election as “a MAGA Warrior.”
Libertarian candidate Doug Mangeris received more than 12,600 votes, well above the 3,352 votes separating Boebert and Laubacher. Elsewhere in Colorado, Republican Rep. Gabe Evans lost the 8th District to Democrat Manny Rutinel, and Democrat Jessica Killin won the 5th District against Rep. Jeff Crank, while Republican Rep. sources.news_title: Lauren Boebert Has A Problem: CNN Just Declared She Has Lost Her Seat in Congress But Won’t Give Up the Midterm Fight
sources.text:
Rep. Lauren Boebert said her Colorado reelection bid was not over on Monday, November 9.
The Republican congresswoman said in an interview with TMZ that ballots awaiting signature corrections, along with military and overseas ballots, were still being processed.
Her opponent, Eileen Laubacher, has already declared victory in the closely fought election while CNN projects the Democrat as the winner.
Boebert Says Remaining Ballots Could Change the Result
On Monday, Boebert told TMZ’s Jacob Wasserman that “the fat lady ain’t sung yet” in Colorado’s 4th congressional district election.
“Do you think I listen to CNN?” the Republican replied when asked about the network’s projection.
Pressed on whether she still believed she could win the election, Boebert replied: “We have thousands of ballots that are being cured. Those are rejected ballots, and those are being cured. They’ll be counted Friday. There’s [sic] also military and overseas ballots that are still coming in. So there are thousands of ballots.”
She continued: “If it changes the outcome, it changes the outcome. And if not, we’ll accept the decision.”
Boebert Denies Exhausting Campaign
The 4th district has been one of the closest in the state and is the only Colorado ballot the Associated Press still hasn’t called.
The Democratic Party has taken all but one of the seven declared results so far, with Jeff Hurd the sole Colorado Republican winner in the 3rd district.
Despite switching to a more conservative-leaning seat in 2024, Boebert has fought a grueling reelection campaign against Laubacher. However, she denied that it had drained her in the TMZ interview.
“I don’t think the campaign was exhausting. I’ve been living this life for seven years on the road and with my voters and having these same meetings, traveling, driving tens of thousands of miles,” she said near the steps of the House of Representatives. “It’s just been part of my life.”
She instead laughed that a Frontier Airlines flight back to Washington had been more exhausting than her reelection campaign.
Defeat Could Be “Liberating”
Boebert jokingly offered her condolences to her Republican colleagues when pressed on the prospect of her tenure in Congress ending.
“It’s almost liberating in a sense, right?” she told Wasserman. “I want to offer condolences to some of my friends that did win.”
However, she maintained that the contest was “not over yet.” She also praised her staff, telling TMZ that she hoped they could find good roles if her Democratic opponent were declared the winner.
“Elections matter, but this doesn’t change who I am and what I do. I’m still going to be aggressive. I’ve always just done really big things and have been pretty successful in them,m and I’m going to continue to do that,” Boebert added.
Uncertainty Continues as Laubacher Claims Victory
While Colorado’s 4th district has still not been called by several news outlets, CNN bucked the trend by declaring Laubacher as the victor on Monday. The Democrat said in a social media post that she was “honored by the trust” voters had placed in her, adding that the campaign was “never about party labels” but “putting people first.”
She continued: “This victory is historic. But making history means nothing if we don’t make a difference. My focus is simple: lower costs, protect healthcare, strengthen rural communities, take on corruption in both parties, and hold Washington accountable.”
Last week, Boebert’s campaign attorney Scott Gessler said later ballot returns had narrowed the deficit between the two candidates.
In a statement, Gessler said: “A significant number of votes remain outstanding in the race. We are fighting for every vote and will continue to ensure every legal vote is counted. Since election night, ballot returns have been trending in Congresswoman Boebert’s direction, consistently lowering the margin under one percentage point.”
He continued: “We are investigating some very unusual voting patterns and expect this election to head to a recount, one way or another.”
Under Colorado state law, a recount is required when the difference between the two leading candidates is no more than half a percent of the leading candidate’s vote total. A losing candidate or another eligible interested party can also request a recount outside that threshold, at its own expense, and must submit the request by November 25.

sources.text:
Rep. Lauren Boebert is holding off on a concession in her race for Colorado’s 4th Congressional District as ballots continue to be processed, The Mirror reports. While Democrat Eileen Laubacher leads the count with 48.8 percent against Boebert’s 47.9 percent, the race remains uncalled by the Associated Press. Current tallies show roughly 98 percent of the ballots have been counted, but the Republican incumbent maintains that the path to a final result is still active.
Boebert addressed the situation in a video posted to her X account. She pushed back against premature declarations of a winner, noting that many ballots are still in the process of being finalized. “There are thousands that still need curing,” she said, adding, “declaring a victory now is like icing a cake before it comes out of the oven.”
The sentiment was echoed during a conversation in DC with TMZ’s Jacob Wasserman. When asked about the projection, Boebert dismissed the reliance on outside news outlets. “You think I listen to CNN?” she joked. She remained firm that the process must play out fully, stating, “No, no, no, so listen, yes, the fat lady ain’t sung yet. OK, so, anyway, we have thousands of ballots that are being cured. Those are rejected ballots, and those are being cured. They’ll be counted Friday.”
Boebert pointed to specific categories of ballots that could shift the current numbers
The congresswoman mentioned that military and overseas ballots are still arriving, which might impact the final margin. “There’s also military and overseas ballots that are still coming in, so there’s thousands of ballots, you know, and if it changes the outcome, it changes the outcome, and if not, we’ll accept the decision,” she stated.
During the same interview, the conversation shifted toward her experience on the campaign trail. Boebert pushed back on the idea that the work was draining. “I don’t think the campaign was exhausting. I mean, I’ve been living this life for 7 years, on the road and, and with my voters and, and having these same meetings, traveling, driving tens of thousands of miles, and so I mean it’s just been part of my life,” she asserted.
She did share a lighthearted jab regarding her travel, joking, “I’ll tell you what was exhausting, the f**** Frontier flight back to DC this week. Like I did not miss that,” before quickly clarifying, “Yes, yes, well, no, they’re great.”
When asked about her future if the final results do not go in her favor, Boebert emphasized her team and her personal outlook. She noted that her primary concern involves her staff. “I wanna make sure that they get in, in good positions, where those are available and that they’re taken care of, that would be a big priority, other than that, I mean this, this job doesn’t define me.”
She added that her professional drive remains unchanged regardless of the election outcome. “Elections matter, but this doesn’t change who I am and what I do. I’m still going to be aggressive. I’ve always, just done really big things and have been pretty successful in them, and I’m gonna continue to do that.”
Before departing, she offered a quick quip when asked about her next career move. Boebert jokingly suggested, “I’m gonna arm wrestle Haley Stevens for your job.”

This story was first published at Colorado Newsline.
DENVER | Democrat Eileen Laubacher declared victory Monday over Republican U.S. Rep. Lauren Boebert in the race to represent Colorado’s 4th Congressional District.
The Associated Press had yet to call the race Monday, when Laubacher had 48.8% of the vote over Boebert’s 47.9%. Libertarian candidate Douglas Mangeris had 3.3% of the vote. The AP estimated 98% of votes in the race were counted at the time.
“Over 17 months, I traveled 40,000 miles across all 21 counties. The message was clear: Coloradans are tired of political games, broken promises, and being ignored by Washington,” Laubacher said in a statement. “They want someone who will fight for them and deliver results.”
Laubacher attended orientation for new members of Congress Monday.
Scott Gessler, an attorney for Boebert’s campaign who represented President Donald Trump during a lawsuit that sought to remove him from the ballot in 2024, said in a statement last week that the campaign will fight to ensure every “legal vote” is counted, and it was “investigating some very unusual voting patterns.” Boebert voted against certifying results from the 2020 election, which former President Joe Biden won.
Boebert’s campaign did not immediately respond to Newsline’s request for comment.
The 4th District, which includes most of Douglas County and the Eastern Plains, has in recent years been considered Colorado’s most conservative district. While the district was previously considered safely Republican, some analyses of the Boebert-Laubacher race recently put the district in the “leans Republican” category.
National Democrats looking to flip the district named it a top priority this election. The last Democrat to represent the district was former U.S. Rep. Betsy Markey, who was elected in 2008. She served one term.
Laubacher, a first-time candidate, is a retired Navy rear admiral and former National Security Council official. She was a longtime Republican but switched her party affiliation, first to unaffiliated, and then to Democratic in 2024. She defended that action at a debate against Boebert by saying her belief in personal liberties is currently found in the Democratic Party and that the GOP she historically supported is “nearly unrecognizable.”
Boebert, of Windsor, was first elected to represent the 3rd District on the Western Slope, but she moved across the state after two terms when she nearly lost reelection in 2022. She is a longtime ally of President Donald Trump, but a rift arose earlier this year when Boebert campaigned alongside outgoing Kentucky U.S. Rep. Thomas Massie, whom the president targeted for leading efforts to force a vote on releasing the Epstein files last year.
Two other congressional seats in Colorado previously held by Republicans flipped to Democrats in last week’s election as part of a “blue tsunami” that swept the state and the country. Republican Rep. Gabe Evans lost his race to Democrat Manny Rutinel in the 8th District, and Republican Rep. Jeff Crank lost his race to Democrat Jessica Killin in the 5th District. With Boebert’s loss, the state’s congressional delegation will favor Democrats 7-1.

CNN Projects Boebert Loses Colorado’s Reddest District, but Her Campaign Expects a Recount
Rep. Lauren Boebert, R-Colo., will lose her seat in Colorado’s most Republican congressional district to Democrat Eileen Laubacher, CNN’s Decision Desk projected Monday, though the Associated Press has not called the race.
Laubacher, a retired Navy rear admiral, will flip the 4th District and deny Boebert a fourth term, CNN reported. The network made its projection Monday afternoon, nearly a week after Election Day.
Laubacher led with 48.8% of the vote to Boebert’s 47.9%, a margin of 3,237 votes, with the Associated Press estimating about 98% of the vote counted, The Denver Post reported. Laubacher declared victory the same day.
“The way we won this race is the way I intend to continue serving the people, which is going everywhere, talking a little bit and listening a lot,” Laubacher told The Denver Post. She said Boebert had not called to concede.
The Associated Press, which calls a race only when the trailing candidate no longer has a path to victory, still listed the contest as too close to call Monday, 9News reported. The Denver station relies on the Associated Press for race calls.
Ballots still being counted include those from military and overseas voters, which must arrive by Thursday. Thursday is also the deadline for voters to fix signature problems or missing ID on mail and provisional ballots.
Counties must finish their count by Friday. Under Colorado law, an automatic recount happens only if the margin falls within half of 1% of the leader’s total, about 929 votes, far less than the current gap.
Boebert’s campaign has signaled it will keep fighting. Scott Gessler, a former Colorado secretary of state who is representing the campaign, said last week that it was “investigating some very unusual voting patterns and expect this election to head to a recount, one way or another.”
Gessler did not say what patterns the campaign was examining, Democracy Docket reported. Campaigns may request a recount at their own expense between Nov. 13 and Nov. 25.
Secretary of State Jena Griswold, a Democrat, defended the count. “Colorado’s elections are safe, secure and accurate – and every voter’s voice will be heard,” she said in a statement cited by Democracy Docket.
A spokesman said the Boebert campaign had not contacted her office about its concerns.
The loss would end a turbulent run for one of the most recognizable members of the House GOP’s MAGA wing.
Boebert switched to the 4th District in 2024 after beating Democrat Adam Frisch by only 546 votes in the 3rd District in 2022, CNN noted.
Her ties to President Donald Trump were rocky this year. In May, Trump called her “weak-minded” and a “carpetbagger” after she backed the release of the Jeffrey Epstein files and campaigned for Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., The Denver Post reported.
Three days before the election, Trump endorsed her anyway, calling her “a MAGA Warrior.”
Laubacher, a former Republican who became a Democrat recently, far outraised Boebert and ran on affordability. She has described herself as “a very moderate person” and said she wants to roll back tariffs and end the war in Iran.
The district, which covers the Eastern Plains and parts of metro Denver, has sent a Democrat to Congress only once in the last 53 years, and only for one term.
Colorado Republicans have taken other losses. Rep. Gabe Evans lost the 8th District on election night, The Denver Post reported.
The Associated Press called the 5th District for Democrat Jessica Killin on Thursday and declared Republican Rep. Jeff Hurd the winner in the 3rd District on Friday.

Laubacher traveled to Washington, D.C. to attend new-member orientation, signaling her confidence that she will be heading to Congress to represent CD-4 for the next two years.
"I know the work is really just beginning," Laubacher told CBS Colorado.

"It is pretty remarkable. It is a great feeling," Laubacher said.

Colorado law requires an automatic recount when the margin between candidates is less than half of 1% of the winning candidate's total votes.
Matt Crane, executive director of the Colorado County Clerks Association, said a candidate who loses by a margin outside that threshold can still request a recount.
"The losing candidate can certainly request a recount at their expense," Crane said.
Crane said Colorado's election system is secure, reliable and transparent. He also does not anticipate a recount would change the outcome of the race.
"I do expect the outcome to say the same," Crane said. "I'm not aware of a recount ever changing the outcome of an election."
Laubacher was asked about the possibility of a recount and said the process is important regardless of the final outcome.
"I think the most important thing is the people of Colorado, the voters, are heard. I think the most important thing is we get these great results and people know their votes mattered. And, I think we have a good system in place that ensures that. That is the most important thing," Laubacher said.

Laubacher is a retired US Navy rear admiral who served for 34 years, building a career in military leadership, international security and diplomacy. According to her official Navy biography, she deployed to Afghanistan in 2009 and later served as Senior Defence Official and Defence Attaché to India from June 2019 to June 2022.
In that role, she represented US defence interests in India and worked on military and security cooperation between the two countries. She subsequently joined the National Security Council as Senior Director for South Asia, serving from October 2022 to May 2024. She retired from the Navy in October 2024.
Laubacher drew on this experience during her congressional campaign, presenting her record in military and government service as a key qualification for public office. She also emphasised affordability and leadership, addressing concerns she said were important to voters in Colorado's 4th Congressional District.
Boebert's Political Career Faces Setback
Boebert was first elected to Congress in 2020 after defeating Republican incumbent Scott Tipton in Colorado's 3rd Congressional District primary. She moved to the 4th District ahead of the 2024 election and won against Democrat Trisha Calvarese with 53.6% of the vote.
